university: The University of Texas at Austin

documents.unit: Office of the Executive Vice President and Provost, Office of Academic Technology
documents.title: AI for Teaching & Learning Toolkit: Policy & Recommendations
documents.summary: The Provost's toolkit page links to campus guidance and answers FAQs. It requires every syllabus to carry an AI policy, allows instructors to require AI where essential, does not endorse detectors, and asks for human review of AI used in grading.
documents.stance_why: The page says "Every syllabus must include a course AI policy that designates whether AI is permitted, prohibited, or partially permitted", so the university sets no single rule and hands the decision to each course.

units.why: The page frames itself as the university's collected guidance: "has issued guidance on many aspects of generative AI". It sets the scope of the toolkit for the whole campus, so a framework statement (P56) addressed to all, general phase, informs.
units.anchor: has issued guidance on many aspects of generative AI and other AI technologies on campus
units.frag_start: The University of Texas at Austin

units.why: The FAQ says "UT does not endorse AI-detection software and holds no central contract for it." That is the university declining to back detectors, which is the P39 idea (not relying on detectors); it is a statement of fact so informs.
units.anchor: UT does not endorse AI-detection software and holds no central contract for it.
units.fit_note: Says the university does not endorse or contract for detectors; it does not say detector output cannot be used as proof.

units.why: "Every syllabus must include a course AI policy" is a mandate on instructors to state AI expectations in the syllabus, so P09 with must. It also fixes three categories (permitted, prohibited, partially permitted), but the core rule is the syllabus requirement, which is why P09 rather than P05.
units.anchor: Every syllabus must include a course AI policy that designates whether AI is permitted
units.policy: Every syllabus must include a course AI policy that designates whether AI is permitted, prohibited, or partially permitted, with clear conditions for use.

units.why: "give written instructions on what is allowed and how students should disclose their use" tells instructors who permit AI what to put in writing. It is about communicating expectations, so P09 rather than P24 (which binds students to disclose).
units.anchor: give written instructions on what is allowed and how students should disclose their use
units.policy: Instructors who permit or partially permit AI give written instructions on what is allowed and how students should disclose their use.

units.why: "UT Austin provides free access to a variety of AI tools" is an institution-wide provision of tools at no cost, which P92 (university-provided tools, not one course) covers. P17 does not fit because it is not course-specific.
units.anchor: UT Austin provides free access to a variety of
units.policy: UT Austin provides free access to a variety of AI tools.

units.why: "UT Sage lets you design custom tutors that can be accessed by students in Canvas" describes a university-provided platform for course-specific tutor bots, the P17 example.
units.anchor: UT Sage lets you design custom tutors that can be accessed by students in Canvas

units.why: Instructors may require generative AI "if such use is essential to the assessment of course learning outcomes". This permits requiring AI under a condition, so P79 (require AI in coursework), modality may, stance require.
units.anchor: Yes, if such use is essential to the assessment of course learning outcomes.

units.why: "we suggest that instructors provide accommodations to students with reasonable objections" is an equity/alternative-access rule for recommended-but-not-required AI tools, P51, with should.
units.anchor: we suggest that instructors provide accommodations to students with reasonable objections
units.policy: Where AI tools are recommended but not required, instructors should provide accommodations to students with reasonable objections.

units.why: "The Office of Academic Technology recommends that appropriate citations and AI disclosure statements be included in significant work products." Students are asked to disclose in submissions, so P24 with should.
units.anchor: recommends that appropriate citations and AI disclosure statements be included in significant work products
units.policy: Appropriate citations and AI disclosure statements are included in significant work products.

units.why: "Diligence about transparent use is a key aspect of AI fluency" gives the reason for disclosure by tying it to AI fluency as a skill. Nearest type is P44 (AI use as a professional skill), though the passage is about transparency, hence a fit note.
units.anchor: Diligence about transparent use is a key aspect of AI fluency.
units.fit_note: Frames transparent disclosure itself as part of AI fluency; it does not claim employers expect AI skills.

units.why: "Check your discipline's or professional organization's style guide" sends people to external style guides for how to disclose AI use. It is a disclosure form rule, nearest P24; no tool/prompt detail is specified so not P25.
units.anchor: many reasons to think twice before automating aspects of the teaching and feedback
units.frag_end: disclose AI use in your context.
units.fit_note: Defers the format of disclosure to disciplinary style guides rather than stating a disclosure rule.

units.why: "There are many reasons to think twice before automating aspects of the teaching and feedback process" advises instructors against automating grading/feedback without prohibiting it; it is a rule on instructor AI use, P59 (P46 is the human-grades rule, which this does not state).
units.anchor: many reasons to think twice before automating aspects of the teaching and feedback process
units.fit_note: Cautions rather than forbids or permits automating teaching and feedback.

units.why: The toolkit quotes Texas law: AI "must not autonomously make or be a controlling factor in making consequential decisions without meaningful human review", naming grading and evaluation of academic work. This is about decisions about people, so P73; P46 is the narrower grading-only rule and this covers more (curriculum, research).
units.anchor: you should exercise the practice of human-in-the-loop when you do use AI tools
units.policy: AI tools must not autonomously make or be a controlling factor in making consequential decisions without meaningful human review; the decisions include grading, the evaluation of academic work, the development of curriculum and teaching materials, and the conducting of research.

units.why: "you should exercise the practice of human-in-the-loop... making sure that you review all output since you are solely responsible" sets conditions for instructors using AI in teaching or grading (human review, sole responsibility), so P101.
units.anchor: you should exercise the practice of human-in-the-loop when you do use AI tools
units.policy: Instructors who use AI tools exercise human-in-the-loop, review all output, and are solely responsible for the result.

units.why: "generative AI tools do not, by design, consistently and reliably produce the same output every time" explains why generative AI is a poor fit for systematic grading. It conditions AI-assisted grading, nearest P101, but is a reason not a rule, hence fit note.
units.anchor: If you need help understanding what kinds of artificial intelligence is being used
units.fit_note: States why generative AI is unreliable for grading and that systematic machine-learning grading may be acceptable; no explicit condition.

units.why: "please reach out to the Office of Academic Technology" offers instructors help understanding AI in academic technology tools, which is support for faculty (P63).
units.anchor: reporting an incident of academic misconduct like unauthorized use of AI

units.why: The link description for Resolving Academic Misconduct names "unauthorized use of AI" as an incident of academic misconduct reported through Student Affairs. That classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: reporting an incident of academic misconduct like unauthorized use of AI
units.policy: Unauthorized use of AI is an incident of academic misconduct, reported through the Division of Student Affairs process.

units.why: The Graduate Education link offers "recommendations for departments creating and maintaining generative AI policies for graduate students". Departments are expected to set their own graduate AI policies, nearest P85; it also mentions maintaining them, but the main point is unit-level policy-making.
units.anchor: recommendations for departments creating and maintaining generative AI policies for graduate students
units.fit_note: Offers recommendations to departments rather than stating they may set their own rules.

units.why: "Become familiar with uses of AI that are allowable and prohibited under University guidance and state law" asks users to know and follow existing university and state rules on AI, P77.
units.anchor: uses of AI that are allowable and prohibited under University guidance and state law

units.why: The Decision Matrix link says it helps users "Understand what kinds of data can be used with which tools", a data-protection and approved-tool pointer, P50.
units.anchor: Understand what kinds of data can be used with which tools.

documents.title: Acceptable Use of Generative AI Tools
documents.summary: The Information Security Office's acceptable-use page sorts AI use by data classification and bans unauthorized tools for sensitive data. It adds a Texas-law bar on AI controlling consequential decisions without human review and a CISO review step.
documents.stance_why: The page lets people use AI tools with conditions on data: public data "may be used freely with AI tools" while Confidential data needs contracted tools, so AI use is permitted with limits. It sets no course-level stance.

units.why: The page says it "outlines acceptable practices for utilizing generative AI tools while safeguarding institutional, personal, and proprietary information", stating the purpose and scope of the guidance, P56.
units.anchor: outlines acceptable practices for utilizing generative AI tools while safeguarding institutional, personal, and proprietary information

units.why: "developed collaboratively by the Office of Legal Affairs, University Compliance Services, the Information Security Office, and the Business Contracts Office" says which bodies made the guidance, P84.
units.anchor: developed collaboratively by the Office of Legal Affairs, University Compliance Services, the Information Security Office

units.why: "Additional guidance may be forthcoming as circumstances evolve" says the guidance is provisional, P54.
units.anchor: Additional guidance may be forthcoming as circumstances evolve.

units.why: Public or Published data "may be used freely with AI tools": a permission with no tool restriction, in the data-protection scheme, P50.
units.anchor: may be used freely with AI tools
units.policy: Data that is publicly available or classified as Published university information may be used freely with AI tools.
units.fit_note: A permission for low-risk data rather than a protection; it is the permissive end of the data classification rule.

units.why: Controlled or Confidential data can be used only with "AI tools that are managed by the university and covered by contracts explicitly protecting university data". This limits sensitive data to vetted tools, P50.
units.anchor: AI tools that are managed by the university and covered by contracts explicitly protecting

units.why: "web search functionality must be disabled" adds a configuration requirement when Confidential data goes into a managed AI tool. Nearest P50 (protect data); the specific requirement is more than the type says.
units.anchor: web search functionality must be disabled
units.fit_note: A concrete technical condition (disable web search, no training, isolated instance) on contracted tools.

units.why: The Decision Matrix "provides information on AI tools and the types of university data authorized for use with each tool", pointing to the list of authorized tools, P92.
units.anchor: information on AI tools and the types of university data authorized for use

units.why: "use should be consistent with the Acceptable Use Policy" requires AI use to follow an existing university policy, P77.
units.anchor: use should be consistent with the Acceptable Use Policy
units.frag_start: In all cases, use should be
units.frag_end: consistent with the Acceptable Use Policy

units.why: Tools without a contract "are not approved for use with Controlled or Confidential university information", a prohibition tied to vetting, P50 (P92 is the positive duty to use approved tools).
units.anchor: AI tools that lack a university contract and appropriate data-sharing controls are not approved

units.why: The prohibited list explicitly includes "AI Detection software" among unauthorized tools for confidential data. It relates to detectors (P39) but is a data restriction, hence fit note.
units.anchor: free or non-UT-managed versions of AI tools like ChatGPT and Copilot, and AI Detection software
units.fit_note: Bars AI detection software from use with Controlled or Confidential data; it does not say detectors are unreliable.

units.why: "Student records subject to FERPA, health information, proprietary information... must not be used with unauthorized AI tools" is a strict privacy ban, P50.
units.anchor: must not be used with unauthorized AI tools

units.why: Texas law "prohibits state agencies, including UT Austin, from deploying AI intended to autonomously make or be a controlling factor in making consequential decisions without meaningful human review". Human review for decisions about people, P73.
units.anchor: prohibits state agencies, including UT Austin, from deploying AI intended to autonomously make

units.why: "UT Austin's CISO must review AI tools to be used for any of these purposes prior to their procurement, development, deployment, or use" is an institutional review requirement, P65.
units.anchor: CISO must review AI tools to be used for any of these purposes prior to

units.why: "AI tools must not be used for activities that are illegal, fraudulent, or violate any state or federal laws, or UT Austin or UT System policies" is a general conduct ban; P74 (fraud) chosen over P77 because the heading and core concern is illegal and fraudulent activity.
units.anchor: AI tools must not be used for activities that are illegal, fraudulent
units.policy: AI tools must not be used for activities that are illegal, fraudulent, or violate any state or federal laws, or UT Austin or UT System policies.
units.fit_note: Also bans violating laws and university policies (P77 territory).

units.why: Click-through agreements "may result in personal responsibility for compliance with the terms and conditions of the AI tool", a warning about tool terms of use, nearest P52.
units.anchor: accepting click-through agreements without delegated signature authority may result in personal responsibility
units.frag_end: terms and conditions of the AI tool.
units.fit_note: About personal liability for terms of use, not copyright or ownership of outputs.

units.why: "ensure compliance with IRUSP Standard 22" for AI tools from external vendors is a vendor and third-party review requirement, P65.
units.anchor: ensure compliance with IRUSP Standard 22

units.why: The page invites readers to "Explore the UT.AI Hub for solutions, training, and community conversations", offering AI training and community resources, P70.
units.anchor: Explore the UT.AI Hub for solutions, training, and community conversations

notes: Course layer deferred in collect file. Page 1 is mostly a link list; only substantive statements coded. Revision history in doc 2 not coded (repeats).
